claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by dislocation accumulation at nanoscale interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion causes dislocations to accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Compositional complexity causes dislocations to accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation pile-ups create localized stress concentrations.
Localized stresses from dislocation pile-ups trigger interface-mediated grain-boundary sliding.
Interface-mediated grain-boundary sliding progressively softens the multilayer.
The starting material is a nanoscale coating with alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer has a nanocrystalline structure.
The starting multilayer has a relatively uniform distribution of dislocation sources.
At 500–700°C, dislocation mobility is active while sufficient microstructural integrity can be retained.
Severe lattice distortion impedes individual dislocation motion in high-entropy alloys.
Compositional complexity impedes individual dislocation motion in high-entropy alloys.
Resistance to dislocation motion causes dislocations to pile up at rigid FCC/BCC layer interfaces.
Increasing local dislocation density eventually triggers grain-boundary sliding at the interfaces.
Multilayers will develop higher localized interfacial dislocation densities than homogeneous monolithic HEA films.
Multilayers will exhibit an earlier onset of grain-boundary sliding than homogeneous monolithic HEA films.
Under constant stress, the multilayers will progressively lose yield strength relative to their initial state.
Enhanced plastic flow will be localized at the layer interfaces.
The proposed mechanism will dominate while individual layer thickness remains nanoscale.
The proposed response may deviate when layer thickness increases substantially or temperature falls outside 500–700°C.
